strengths: The paper proposes a clear and appealing test-time mechanism for producing region-specific embeddings from frozen vision-language encoders by optimizing a token so that its explainability map matches a query mask. This is a meaningful alternative to pixel-space prompting or model finetuning.

The method is broadly applicable as a drop-in replacement for CLIP-style visual embeddings, and the paper demonstrates this across referring expression retrieval, localized class retrieval, captioning, and qualitative diffusion examples.

The empirical results on referring expression retrieval and class retrieval are strong, especially against reproduced baselines under the same mask-based evaluation setting. The scaling results across ViT-B/32, ViT-B/16, ViT-L/14, and ViT-H/14 are also encouraging.
The gradient decomposition idea is practically useful for multiple masks per image, and the runtime ablation shows that it can substantially reduce cost when many masks are processed.

The paper includes relevant ablations on mask quality and explainability method choice, and it explicitly discusses some limitations such as dependence on suitable explainability methods and reduced resolution for small objects.
weaknesses: The main evaluation relies heavily on provided ground-truth or candidate masks, which limits conclusions about end-to-end practical performance. Comparisons to methods using region proposals or different evaluation protocols are difficult to interpret, even though the paper marks some of these differences.

The method depends strongly on the choice of explainability method. The ablation shows LeGrad is dramatically better than GradCAM and CheferCAM, which weakens the claim that MaskInversion can generally work with any differentiable explainability method.

The localized captioning evaluation is not fully convincing: correctness is measured indirectly through CLIP text-embedding similarity to referring expressions, rather than standard captioning metrics or human evaluation. This may reward CLIP-aligned phrasing rather than genuinely accurate captions.
The localized diffusion results are purely qualitative and limited. They support intuition about the learned embeddings but do not substantiate strong claims about image generation applications.

The test-time optimization cost remains a concern. Although gradient decomposition helps for many masks, the method still requires iterative optimization per image/mask and is slower and more complex than single-forward baselines, especially for interactive or dense settings.

Some technical and presentation details need tightening: the gradient decomposition derivation omits discussion of nonlinearities and normalization in the explainability pipeline, hyperparameter choices are only partially justified, and there are table/text inconsistencies and typos such as the apparent PascalVOC Acc@10 value of 8.9 for ViT-B/32 MaskInversion and the appendix describing the explainability ablation as MSCOCO while the table says PascalVOC.

Reproducibility is incomplete from the manuscript alone: implementation details such as optimization stability, learning rates, exact preprocessing, mask resizing, prompt templates, and code availability are not described in enough detail for confident replication.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: deriving region-specific representations from frozen vision-language models without additional training.
The core idea of optimizing a localized embedding so that its explainability map matches a query mask is intuitive and potentially useful as a test-time adaptation mechanism.

The paper evaluates across several downstream settings, including referring expression retrieval, class retrieval, localized captioning, and qualitative diffusion examples, rather than only a single benchmark.
The comparison includes several relevant baselines such as cropping, masked cropping, visual prompting methods, RIS, and AlphaCLIP, and the reported class/retrieval numbers are often strong.
The mask-quality and explainability-method ablations are useful and reveal important practical dependencies of the approach.
weaknesses: The novelty is limited. The method is essentially test-time embedding optimization using an attribution loss, combining known ideas from textual inversion, saliency optimization, and region prompting. The paper does not convincingly establish that this is a substantial conceptual advance over existing visual prompting or mask-conditioned CLIP methods.

The central technical claim is under-supported. The gradient decomposition derivation appears oversimplified, especially for cosine similarity and normalization, and the paper does not provide enough validation that the approximation is exact, stable, or generally applicable beyond the chosen setup.

The method depends heavily on the availability and quality of query masks, yet much of the evaluation assumes ground-truth masks. This weakens the practical significance, since obtaining high-quality masks is itself a major part of the problem.

The claimed generality to “any pre-trained model” is not demonstrated. Experiments are essentially CLIP/ViT-centric and rely strongly on LeGrad; the ablation shows performance collapses with other explainability methods, which undermines the generality claim.

Several evaluations are not fully convincing. Localized captioning uses an indirect CLIP-similarity retrieval metric rather than standard captioning metrics or human evaluation, and localized diffusion is only qualitative.

The baseline comparisons are somewhat messy and potentially unfair: reported and reproduced settings differ, some baselines use different backbones or proposal mechanisms, and scaling to larger CLIP backbones may conflate the method’s benefit with backbone strength.

The paper lacks important reproducibility details, including a missing/blank project page, incomplete hyperparameter sensitivity analysis, unclear runtime/memory costs for realistic mask counts, and limited implementation detail for optimization stability.

The presentation quality is below the expected standard: there are many typos and grammatical issues, table inconsistencies such as an apparent erroneous Acc@10 value in Table 2, and vague or overstated claims such as seamless drop-in replacement across applications.

The strongest empirical gains are on settings where the method receives the object mask as input, so the results do not clearly show that the learned embedding captures semantics beyond being forced to attend to the provided region.

The limitations section acknowledges dependence on explainability methods and resolution, but does not adequately address broader failure modes such as small objects, multiple overlapping regions, noisy masks, computational cost, or cases where attribution maps are not semantically faithful.

strengths: The paper proposes a clear and useful test-time method for producing mask-conditioned localized embeddings from frozen vision-language models, avoiding backbone fine-tuning while remaining compatible with downstream systems that consume CLIP-style image embeddings.

The core idea of optimizing a localized embedding token so that its explainability map matches a query mask is conceptually elegant and practically appealing as a drop-in replacement for the global CLS token.

The evaluation is broad: referring expression retrieval, region-level class retrieval, localized captioning, localized diffusion visualizations, mask-quality ablations, backbone scaling, and runtime analysis are all considered.

Results are consistently strong across several datasets and backbones, often outperforming reproduced baselines such as crop, masked crop, RedCircle, FGVP, RIS, and AlphaCLIP, including in zero-shot settings without fine-tuning.

The gradient decomposition for amortizing explanation-map computation across masks is a valuable practical contribution, and the paper includes runtime evidence showing benefits when many masks are processed per image.
The paper is generally well motivated and positions the method well relative to visual prompting and fine-tuned mask-aware CLIP variants.
weaknesses: The method depends heavily on the quality and suitability of the chosen explainability method; the appendix shows performance drops dramatically with alternatives to LeGrad, which weakens the claim of broad applicability to arbitrary frozen foundation models.

The mathematical presentation of the gradient decomposition seems underspecified: the decomposition appears to ignore details of cosine normalization and explanation-map postprocessing, so it is not fully clear under what exact assumptions the stated simplification is valid.

The comparison to prior work is somewhat difficult to interpret because some reported baselines use different evaluation settings, model combinations, or region proposal assumptions. The reproduced comparisons help, but the paper would benefit from an even cleaner apples-to-apples protocol.

Localized captioning is evaluated with an indirect CLIP text-similarity retrieval metric rather than human evaluation or standard captioning metrics adapted to regions, so the quantitative evidence for this application is weaker than for retrieval/classification.

The diffusion application is mostly qualitative; it helps illustrate the embedding behavior but does not provide rigorous evidence that the learned localized embeddings improve generation quality or controllability.

The method performs per-mask test-time optimization, which may be limiting for latency-sensitive applications. The runtime ablation is useful, but more discussion of absolute throughput, memory cost, and comparison to single-forward learned alternatives would strengthen the practical case.

Several presentation issues remain, including typos, awkward phrasing, and apparent table inconsistencies such as the PascalVOC B/32 Acc@10 value reported as 8.9, which likely should be 98.9. These do not undermine the main idea but reduce polish and reproducibility confidence.

strengths: The paper proposes a clear and interesting test-time method for obtaining mask-conditioned regional embeddings from a frozen vision-language model, using explainability-map optimization rather than retraining or modifying image pixels.

The method is practically appealing: it is backbone-preserving, can serve as a drop-in replacement for CLIP-style visual embeddings, and is demonstrated across classification, referring expression retrieval, captioning, and diffusion-based visualization.

The empirical section is broad and includes several relevant baselines, including visual prompting methods, AlphaCLIP, RIS, MaskCLIP, CLIPSurgery, and SCLIP. The reported gains on class retrieval and referring expression retrieval are often substantial.

The paper includes useful ablations on mask quality, regularization strength, optimization iterations, runtime, gradient decomposition, and choice of explainability method, which helps clarify when the method works.
The gradient decomposition is a sensible engineering contribution that makes multi-mask inference more efficient, and the runtime analysis supports its usefulness for images with many masks.
weaknesses: The main evaluation relies heavily on ground-truth or high-quality masks, so the practical end-to-end value is somewhat overstated. The Box and Box+SAM ablation helps, but the core comparisons mostly assume a strong mask oracle.

Several tasks are somewhat custom or indirect. Localized captioning is evaluated through CLIP text retrieval against referring expressions rather than standard caption quality metrics or human evaluation, making the claimed captioning capability less convincing.

The method depends strongly on the chosen explainability method: LeGrad vastly outperforms GradCAM and CheferCAM. This makes the generality claim weaker, especially for non-ViT backbones or models without high-quality differentiable attribution methods.

Some SOTA comparisons are difficult to interpret because prior methods use different settings, model sizes, proposal mechanisms, or supervision regimes. The paper acknowledges this in part, but the SOTA claims remain stronger than the evidence warrants.

The learned embedding is optimized to match an attribution map to a mask, but the paper gives limited analysis of failure modes where this objective yields attribution alignment without semantic faithfulness. More qualitative failures and robustness tests would strengthen the technical case.

Reproducibility details are incomplete for a top-tier submission: hyperparameters beyond iteration count and alpha are sparse, compute cost is only partially characterized, and it is unclear whether code, exact splits, and prompt templates will be released.

The method requires per-mask optimization at test time, which may be costly for dense or interactive applications despite the proposed speedup. The runtime comparison is useful but not extensive enough across backbones, resolutions, and hardware.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: obtaining region-specific representations from frozen vision-language models without finetuning the backbone.
The core idea of optimizing a localized embedding so that its explainability map matches a query mask is interesting and reasonably easy to understand.

The empirical section covers several downstream settings, including referring expression retrieval, class retrieval, localized captioning, and qualitative diffusion examples, rather than evaluating only one narrow task.

The paper includes comparisons to several relevant mask-conditioned or training-free CLIP baselines, as well as some useful ablations on mask quality, the regularization weight, explainability method choice, and runtime decomposition.
The method has an appealing practical property in principle: it can be applied at test time to frozen CLIP-style models and can reuse the resulting token as a drop-in visual embedding.
weaknesses: The novelty is limited. The method is essentially test-time optimization of an embedding using an attribution-map matching loss, combining existing ingredients such as CLIP embeddings, gradient-based explanations, Dice loss, and textual-inversion-like optimization. The paper does not convincingly establish that this is a substantial conceptual advance over prior localized CLIP prompting, masking, and token/pooling approaches.

The central technical premise is under-validated: matching an explainability map to a mask does not necessarily imply that the optimized token is a faithful or semantically meaningful region representation. The paper reports downstream accuracy but gives little diagnostic evidence that the optimization is not merely exploiting artifacts of the explanation method or CLIP similarity space.

The evaluation relies heavily on ground-truth masks or high-quality mask inputs, which weakens the practical claim. The paper does include a mask-quality ablation, but the main results assume an already localized region, so the method sidesteps a major part of the open-vocabulary localization problem.

Several comparisons are hard to interpret fairly. Some SOTA numbers use different protocols, some baselines are reproduced under the authors' adapted setting, and the strongest results often use larger backbones than many baselines. This makes the magnitude of the claimed SOTA improvement less convincing.

The captioning evaluation is weak. Scoring generated localized captions by CLIP text similarity against referring expressions is an indirect metric that may reward CLIP-space alignment rather than caption correctness, specificity, or linguistic quality. No human evaluation or standard captioning/grounding metric is provided.

The localized diffusion results are purely qualitative and should not be used as strong evidence for the representation quality. They are visually suggestive but do not support broad claims about generation or multi-object understanding.

The method's computational cost remains a concern. Even with gradient decomposition, the approach requires per-image/per-mask test-time optimization, and the runtime analysis is limited; it lacks sufficient hardware details, scaling analysis across backbones/resolutions in the main evaluation, and comparison to simpler one-forward-pass alternatives under matched conditions.

Important reproducibility details are missing or under-specified, including optimization learning rate, prompt templates, exact splits/subsets such as OpenImagesV7, hardware, preprocessing choices, and implementation details for reproduced baselines.

The claims about generality are stronger than the evidence. Although the paper says MaskInversion can work with any differentiable explainability method or pretrained model, the ablation shows performance depends heavily on LeGrad, with other explainability methods performing much worse.

The discussion of limitations is incomplete. It acknowledges dependence on explainability quality and low-resolution CLIP inputs, but does not sufficiently discuss failure cases, sensitivity to mask size/object scale, adversarial or spurious saliency behavior, out-of-manifold optimized embeddings, or the reliability of explanation maps as supervision.

Overall, while the paper is understandable and has some promising empirical results, I do not find the contribution or evidence strong enough for a top-tier AI conference. The method feels incremental, the evaluation has important protocol and metric weaknesses, and several central claims are not fully supported.

strengths: Proposes a clear and useful training-free method for obtaining mask-conditioned localized embeddings from frozen vision-language models by optimizing a learned token against an explainability map.

The method is broadly applicable: the same localized token is evaluated as a drop-in representation for referring expression retrieval, region class retrieval, localized captioning, and qualitative localized diffusion.

Empirical results are strong across multiple datasets and backbones, with consistent gains over reproduced baselines and recent training-free methods; the scaling to larger CLIP backbones is especially compelling.
The paper includes meaningful ablations on mask quality, regularization strength, optimization steps, runtime, gradient decomposition, and explainability method choice.
The gradient decomposition idea is practically important and helps make the otherwise expensive test-time optimization more plausible for images with many masks.
weaknesses: The method depends heavily on the availability and quality of a suitable differentiable explainability method; the ablation shows performance collapses with several alternatives, which limits claims of broad applicability to arbitrary backbones.
Several evaluations assume ground-truth or high-quality masks, so the end-to-end usefulness for realistic open-vocabulary localization pipelines is less fully established.
Localized captioning is evaluated with a proxy CLIP retrieval metric and an older CLIPCap model; this only partially supports claims about captioning quality and regional faithfulness.
The diffusion experiments are qualitative only, so they are better viewed as visualization of the embedding than as evidence of strong generative performance.
Runtime and memory analysis could be deeper, especially for large backbones, high-resolution images, many masks, and the cost of storing or computing the decomposed Jacobian.
Some claims, such as naturally handling overlapping or multi-object masks without interference, are mostly argued from the loss formulation and qualitative examples rather than rigorously evaluated.
